text:
Agroforestry, Soil, Water and Biodiversity

Agroforestry integrates trees and shrubs with crops and/or livestock. It can provide multiple environmental functions including improved soil cover, reduced erosion, improved soil fertility and biological activity, increased organic carbon, more effective use of available water and enhanced biodiversity.

FAO describes agroforestry systems as contributing to soil fertility, water conservation, carbon capture and biodiversity conservation.

Agroforestry can influence water cycling through interception, transpiration and soil water retention. Trees and vegetation can also reduce surface runoff and increase infiltration.

Source:
FAO, Service Functions of Agroforestry Systems.
https://www.fao.org/4/xii/ms20-e.htm

Additional source:
FAO, Agroforestry.
https://www.fao.org/4/i1861e/i1861e.pdf

Key relationships:
- Agroforestry → soil organic matter and carbon.
- Agroforestry → soil structure and infiltration.
- Agroforestry → water retention and reduced runoff.
- Agroforestry → habitat structure and biodiversity.

Climate Change, Land Management and Biodiversity

The IPCC identifies land ecosystems and biodiversity as vulnerable to climate change and climate extremes. Sustainable land management can help address multiple environmental stressors.

The IPCC identifies practices including cover crops, crop residue retention, reduced or zero tillage and maintenance of ground cover as options for reducing vulnerability to soil erosion and nutrient loss.

The IPCC also reports that agroforestry, perennial systems and improved land management can reduce erosion and nutrient leaching while building soil carbon.

Source:
IPCC, Special Report on Climate Change and Land, Summary for Policymakers.
https://www.ipcc.ch/srccl/chapter/summary-for-policymakers/

Additional source:
IPCC AR6 Working Group III, Chapter 7: Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Uses.
https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-7/

Key relationships:
- Climate stress + land degradation → increased ecosystem vulnerability.
- Cover crops → reduced erosion and nutrient loss.
- Agroforestry → soil carbon + erosion reduction + water-related benefits.
- Land management can influence several environmental variables simultaneously.

Soil Organic Carbon and Soil Health

Soil organic carbon (SOC) is a major component of soil organic matter and supports multiple soil functions. FAO reports that SOC helps stabilize soil structure and aggregation, improves nutrient cycling and storage, and can increase soil porosity and water-holding capacity. SOC also provides habitat and food resources for soil organisms, supporting soil biodiversity.

Source:
FAO Global Soil Partnership, Unlocking the Potential of Soil Organic Carbon: A Feasible Way Forward.
https://www.fao.org/fileadmin/user_upload/GSP/docs/Unlocking_SOC.pdf

Key relationships:
- Higher SOC can improve soil structure and aggregation.
- Improved soil structure can support water infiltration and water retention.
- SOC supports soil organisms and soil biological activity.
- Low SOC can reduce resilience to water stress and degradation.

Soil Organic Carbon, Water and Land Degradation

Agricultural soils with depleted organic matter can have reduced ability to hold water and nutrients, reduced rainfall infiltration, greater compaction and loss of soil biodiversity.

Conservation practices that maintain organic matter and soil cover can improve soil functions. FAO describes soil organic matter as important for soil health, water retention, nutrient availability and biological activity.

Source:
FAO, Soil Organic Carbon Accumulation and Greenhouse Gas Emission Reductions from Conservation Agriculture.
https://www.fao.org/4/i2672e/i2672e.pdf

Key relationships:
- Low soil organic matter can reduce water-holding capacity.
- Reduced water retention can increase vulnerability during rainfall shortages.
- Soil degradation can affect soil biodiversity.
- Maintaining soil cover and organic inputs can support soil structure and water-related functions.
